name: NPO (Nothing by Mouth)
definition: No oral intake of any kind — no food, liquids, medications (unless specified), or ice chips, unless specifically ordered otherwise.
rationale: Aspiration risk too high for oral intake
qualifies: Nothing — complete restriction unless items are individually ordered
doesNotQualify: Medications — must be verified with provider individually
nursingImplications: Ensure IV access is patent and IV fluids ordered
Hold all oral medications unless provider specifically clears them — verify individually
Oral care q2–4h — NPO patients are still at risk for mucositis and discomfort
Document last oral intake time
Keep ice water or nothing at bedside (label clearly)
Monitor for hypoglycemia in diabetic patients — notify provider
Educate patient and family about reason for NPO
Document compliance
After midnight NPO: clear communication to next shift
medicationImplications: Confirm with provider and pharmacist which oral medications to hold vs administer via alternative route
Some oral medications can be crushed and given via NG tube
Consider IV alternatives for critical medications

name: Clear Liquid Diet
definition: Liquids that are transparent at room temperature, leave minimal residue, and are easy to digest. Used as a first step in resuming oral intake or for bowel preparation.
nursingImplications: Advance diet if tolerated and per order — do not advance without order
Monitor for nausea/vomiting after initiation
Document tolerance — percentage consumed, any symptoms
Educate patient on what qualifies
Monitor hydration status
Check blood glucose in diabetics — clear liquids are low protein and may cause rapid glucose changes
Avoid progression if signs of aspiration
medicationImplications: Most oral medications can be taken with clear liquids unless otherwise specified
Exception: some medications require food or specific timing — verify with pharmacist

name: Full Liquid Diet
definition: Includes all clear liquids plus creamy or liquid foods that are liquid at room temperature. More nutritionally complete than clear liquids but less so than solid food.
rationale: Transitional diet between clear liquids and soft/regular
nursingImplications: More nutritionally complete — assess if patient is meeting caloric/protein needs
Consult dietitian for extended full liquid diet
Monitor weight
Monitor blood glucose (higher sugar content)

name: Pureed Diet
definition: All foods processed to a smooth, uniform, lump-free consistency. Requires no chewing. For patients with severe dysphagia or inability to chew.
doesNotQualify: Foods that fall apart into pieces
nursingImplications: Speech therapy evaluation typically ordered for dysphagia patients
HOB at 90° or highest possible during meals and 30–60 min after
Monitor for aspiration signs: coughing, wet/gurgly voice after eating, recurrent pneumonias
Aspiration precautions apply
Ensure adequate caloric and protein intake — consult dietitian
Document swallowing tolerance
medicationImplications: Crushed medications can often be mixed into pureed foods unless contraindicated (extended-release)

name: Mechanical Soft Diet
definition: Regular foods that are soft-textured, easy to chew, and cut into small pieces. No raw vegetables, hard fruits, tough meats, or foods requiring extensive chewing.
nursingImplications: Ensure foods are cut into small pieces
Monitor tolerance and intake
May advance to regular diet when tolerated and per order

name: Heart Healthy Diet
definition: Diet low in sodium, saturated fat, trans fat, and cholesterol. Emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins, and healthy fats. Used for cardiovascular disease, CHF, hypertension.
qualifies: Whole grains (oatmeal, brown rice, whole wheat bread)
Healthy fats (olive oil, avocado, nuts — in moderation)
doesNotQualify: High-sodium foods (processed meats, canned soups, fast food)
Saturated fats (butter, red meat, full-fat dairy)
nursingImplications: Teach label reading — sodium hides in processed foods
Sodium limit typically <2g/day for CHF patients
Daily weights — teach patient to report >2 lb gain in 24h
Fluid restriction if ordered (CHF)
Educate on food choices at each meal opportunity
Involve dietitian for comprehensive education
Reinforce at discharge
medicationImplications: Warfarin patients: maintain consistent vitamin K intake — sudden changes in diet affect INR

name: Low Sodium Diet (2g)
definition: Restriction of sodium intake to 2000 mg (2g) per day. Critical in CHF, hypertension, renal failure, liver disease.
qualifies: Fresh or frozen vegetables (no salt added)
Homemade foods with no added salt
doesNotQualify: Table salt and all added salt
nursingImplications: Label reading education (sodium per serving)
Daily weights — same scale, same time, same clothes
Monitor for hypernatremia paradoxically in aggressive diuresis
Educate patient and family — major source of readmission for CHF patients is dietary nonadherence
Involve dietitian

name: Renal Diet (Low Potassium, Low Phosphorus)
definition: Diet restricting potassium, phosphorus, and often sodium. Used in CKD and dialysis patients to prevent dangerous electrolyte imbalances.
qualifies: White bread, white rice (lower phosphorus than whole grains)
doesNotQualify: High potassium: bananas, oranges, potatoes, tomatoes, avocado, beans, nuts
High phosphorus: dairy (milk, cheese, yogurt), dark cola, nuts, beans, whole grains
Salt substitutes — often potassium chloride (very high K+)
nursingImplications: Monitor K+, phosphate, calcium, albumin
Instruct on leaching vegetables (boiling in large water volume to remove K+)
Phosphate binders given with meals — ensure patient takes them
Fluid restriction may also apply
Refer to dietitian for individualized renal diet education
Dialysis patients: timing of diet relative to dialysis sessions matters
medicationImplications: Phosphate binders (sevelamer, calcium carbonate) taken WITH meals to bind phosphorus — timing is critical

name: Diabetic Diet (Carbohydrate Controlled)
definition: Controlled carbohydrate intake typically 45–60g carbohydrates per meal and 15–30g per snack. Consistent timing of meals. Emphasizes low glycemic index foods.
doesNotQualify: White bread, white rice in large portions
nursingImplications: Blood glucose monitoring before meals and 2h after (or per order)
Insulin given relative to meal timing — confirm when patient has food on tray
Hypoglycemia risk if meal delayed — always have fast-acting glucose available
Consistent meal timing helps with glycemic control
Snack may be ordered at bedtime to prevent nocturnal hypoglycemia
Consult dietitian for comprehensive education
Carb counting education at discharge
medicationImplications: Insulin timing critical relative to meal consumption — coordinate meal delivery and insulin administration

name: Nectar-Thick Liquid
definition: Liquids thickened to the consistency of nectar or tomato juice for patients with dysphagia who aspirate thin liquids.
rationale: Dysphagia with aspiration of thin liquids
nursingImplications: Speech therapy evaluation and MBSS/FEES confirms appropriate consistency level
All liquids must be thickened — including water
Educate patient, family, and all staff — any thin liquid is a risk
HOB at highest position possible during intake and 30–60 min after
Monitor for signs of aspiration: coughing, wet voice after drinking
Ice chips not allowed (become thin liquid when melted)
medicationImplications: Liquid medications must be checked with pharmacist for appropriate thickening

name: Honey-Thick Liquid
definition: Liquids thickened to the consistency of honey for patients with more significant swallowing dysfunction than nectar-thick alone addresses.
rationale: Aspiration risk not managed by nectar-thick
nursingImplications: Same as nectar-thick but more restrictive
Dehydration risk with honey-thick — patients often drink less
Monitor hydration status closely
Dietitian and speech therapy collaboration essential

name: TPN (Total Parenteral Nutrition)
definition: Complete nutrition delivered intravenously, bypassing the GI tract entirely. Contains dextrose, amino acids, lipids, electrolytes, vitamins, and minerals.
rationale: Prolonged NPO with inability to use enteral nutrition
nursingImplications: Central venous access required (PICC, CVC) — dedicated TPN lumen
Never hang TPN without pharmacist and provider order verification
Check glucose q4–6h when initiating, then q6–8h when stable
Monitor for hyperglycemia — insulin sliding scale or drip often co-ordered
Strict I&Os
Change TPN tubing q24h with each new bag
Never add anything to TPN bag without pharmacy consultation
Monitor labs: glucose, electrolytes, BMP, LFTs, triglycerides (with lipids), prealbumin weekly
Line care critical — highest infection risk with TPN (glucose-rich medium)
TPN bags must be used within 24h — check expiration before hanging
If TPN must be stopped abruptly: hang D10W at same rate to prevent hypoglycemia
medicationImplications: Do not add medications directly to TPN unless specifically ordered and verified — compatibility issues are complex

name: Enteral Tube Feeding
definition: Nutrition delivered via tube into the stomach or small intestine (NG tube, Dobhoff, G-tube, J-tube). Used when GI tract is functional but patient cannot eat.
nursingImplications: Verify tube placement before each feeding/medication: pH aspirate < 5, or X-ray confirmed
HOB at 30–45° during and 30–60 min after feeding
Check gastric residual per protocol (typically hold if > 200–500 mL per protocol)
Flush tube per order: typically 30 mL water before/after meds and q4–8h during continuous feeding
Monitor for diarrhea, constipation, bloating
Monitor blood glucose
Daily I&Os
Formula-specific guidance per dietitian and order
medicationImplications: Many medications cannot be crushed (extended-release, enteric-coated)
Always verify crushing appropriateness with pharmacist
Flush before and after each medication
Give each medication separately — do not mix multiple crushed medications together
